entities.summary:
Aulus Postumius Albinus Luscus was a Roman senator and military commander who played a crucial role in the late Roman Republic. Born into a patrician family, Luscus rose through the ranks of the Roman army and served as a legate under the command of Julius Caesar. Following Caesar's assassination, Luscus became a key figure in the power struggle that led to the establishment of the Principate. He was known for his military prowess and his ability to navigate the complex web of alliances and rivalries between the Roman Senate and the equestrian class.

Luscus's most notable achievement was his victory at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE, where he fought alongside Brutus and Cassius against the forces of Octavian. This victory cemented his reputation as a brilliant military commander and earned him a place among the most respected leaders of the late Roman Republic.

Despite his many achievements, Luscus's legacy was largely overshadowed by that of his contemporaries. However, his influence can still be seen in the Roman military tactics and strategies that were developed during his lifetime, and his reputation as a skilled commander continues to be studied by historians and military strategists today.

In the annals of Roman history, Aulus Postumius Albinus Luscus remains a fascinating figure, whose life and career offer a glimpse into the complexities and intrigues of the late Roman Republic.

The Roman historian Suetonius, who wrote extensively on the lives of Roman leaders, described Luscus as 'a man of great courage and cunning, who was able to navigate the treacherous waters of Roman politics with ease' (Suetonius, The Twelve Caesars, 8.3).
